title: Biasing Techniques
intro: An amplifier works only if every transistor carries its intended current and has enough terminal voltage to stay saturated. The current fixes $g_m$ and $r_o$; the voltages fix headroom and swing. This page covers common-source stages; the next covers CG, follower and differential stages.

items: Bias with currents copied from a reference, not with fixed voltages: a mirror's output follows the reference, while a fixed gate voltage gives a current that depends on $V_{TH}$, mobility and the supply.
Keep the bias network from loading or fighting the signal: isolate it with a large resistance and couple the signal through a capacitor where needed.
Spend little power on bias: a bias branch current of a tenth to a fifth of the main device's current is typical.
Never leave a gate node floating: it needs a DC path to a defined voltage.

blocks.text: A bias voltage $V_B$ tied directly to the gate would fight the input. Instead couple $V_{in}$ through $C_B$ and feed $V_B$ through a large $R_B$, so node X has $V_B$ at DC and $V_{in}$ at signal frequencies. $C_B$ and $R_B$ form a high-pass filter, so $1/(2\pi R_B C_B)$ must lie below the lowest signal frequency. $V_B$ itself should come from a diode-connected device carrying $I_B$, making M1 a mirror of $M_B$.

blocks.alt: Common-source stage M1 with drain resistor RD. The input Vin connects through capacitor CB to the gate node X. A resistor RB connects X to node VB, which is the gate and drain of diode-connected MB fed by current source IB.
blocks.caption: CS stage biased by a mirror through $R_B$, with AC-coupled input: $I_{D1} = I_B (W/L)_1/(W/L)_B$.

items: For low signal frequencies (audio, for example) $R_B$ and $C_B$ grow large and take a lot of area.
$C_B$ brings its own parasitic capacitance into the signal path, which limits how large it can be even when area is free.

blocks.text: A transistor as the large resistor

When $R_B C_B$ must be large, replace $R_B$ by a long, narrow MOSFET $M_R$ in deep triode with a small overdrive. To keep its overdrive defined across PVT, set its gate-source voltage with a diode-connected device $M_C$ whose $(W/L)_C$ is large, so $V_{GS,C}$ is just above $V_{TH}$. In strong inversion with a long-channel model:

Driving M1's gate from the previous stage's drain removes the capacitor, but then the first stage's bias errors set M1's bias, and in a cascade PVT shifts are amplified exactly like signals. Direct coupling is acceptable when each stage has a low gain (2 or 3); for more stages or higher gains, negative feedback is needed to pin the bias.
CS stage with a current-source load

If both M1 and its PMOS load M2 are mirrored from references, two high-impedance current sources are in series, and any difference between the copied currents drives the output to whichever rail lets them agree, possibly forcing M1 or M2 into triode. The fix is to make M2 diode-connected at DC through a large $R_G$ from the output to its gate, with $C_G$ grounding the gate at signal frequencies. M2 then simply carries whatever M1 sets:

blocks.caption: Choose $R_G \gg r_{o1} \parallel r_{o2}$ and $1/(2\pi R_G C_G)$ below the lowest signal frequency.

blocks.alt: CS stage with NMOS M1 and PMOS load M2. The output node connects through resistor RG to node N at M2's gate, and capacitor CG connects N to ground.
blocks.caption: Self-biased current-source load: diode-connected at DC, a current source at signal frequencies.

blocks.text: The output now idles at $V_{DD} - |V_{GS2}|$, which may not centre the swing. Drawing a small constant current $I_G$ out of $R_G$ keeps $V_N$ low enough for M2's $V_{GS}$ while raising the output to $V_{out} = V_N + I_G R_G$. Choosing $I_G R_G$ to equalise the room above and below centres the swing. Alternatively, size M2 for $|V_{GS2}| \approx V_{DD}/2$ with no $I_G$; the $I_G$ version is often preferred because a larger PMOS overdrive (at the same current) lowers its noise.

An NMOS and a PMOS driven by the same input satisfy $V_{GS1} + |V_{GS2}| = V_{DD}$, so their current is very PVT-sensitive and the two devices also fight. A large feedback resistor $R_F$ from the output to the joined gates diode-connects both at DC (no DC current flows in $R_F$), so they settle at a common current. To set that current precisely, add a current source $I_1$ in M2's source, bypassed by $C_1$ with $1/(C_1\omega_{min}) \ll 1/g_{m2}$ so M2 sees no degeneration in band (at the cost of some headroom). Because the gate bias now tracks the output, the input must be capacitively coupled. With large enough $R_F$, $C_1$ and input capacitor, the in-band gain is $(g_{m1} + g_{m2})(r_{o1} \parallel r_{o2})$.

blocks.title: Divider bias
blocks.text: $V_{DD} = 1.8\text{ V}$. A divider $R_1 = 100\text{ k}\Omega$ (top) and $R_2 = 200\text{ k}\Omega$ (bottom) feeds the gate of an NMOS with its source at ground. If $\mu_n C_{ox}W/L = 2\text{ mA/V}^2$ and $V_{TH} = 0.5\text{ V}$, find $I_D$.
solution: A 50 mV rise in $V_{TH}$ moves $V_{ov}$ to 0.65 V and $I_D$ to 0.42 mA, 14 percent lower. A mirror from a stable reference does much better.

blocks.title: Sizing the coupling network
blocks.text: A CS stage is biased through $R_B = 100\text{ k}\Omega$ and must pass signals down to 1 MHz. What is the minimum $C_B$?
solution: In practice choose several times more, so the corner sits well below 1 MHz and the in-band attenuation is negligible.

blocks.title: MOS resistor value
blocks.text: In the MOS-resistor bias network, $(W/L)_C = 20$, $(W/L)_R = 0.5$ and $g_{m,C} = 0.5\text{ mS}$. Find the on-resistance of $M_R$.

blocks.title: Centring the swing with IG
blocks.text: A self-biased CS stage with a current-source load runs from $V_{DD} = 1.2\text{ V}$. $|V_{GS2}| = 0.8\text{ V}$ with $|V_{TH2}| = 0.5\text{ V}$, and M1 needs 0.2 V of $V_{DS}$. (a) Without $I_G$, what peak-to-peak swing is possible? (b) What $I_G R_G$ centres the swing, and what swing results?
solution: (a) The output idles at $1.2 - 0.8 = 0.4\text{ V}$. It can fall to 0.2 V (0.2 V of room) and rise to $1.2 - 0.3 = 0.9\text{ V}$ (0.5 V of room). The smaller room limits a symmetric swing to $2 \cdot 0.2 = 0.4\text{ V}$ peak-to-peak.
(b) Centre between 0.2 V and 0.9 V: 0.55 V, so $I_G R_G = 0.15\text{ V}$ (for example $0.75\,\mu\text{A}$ through 200 kΩ). Each side then has 0.35 V, giving 0.7 V peak-to-peak.
blocks.answer: (a) 0.4 V; (b) shift by 0.15 V for 0.7 V peak-to-peak.
